ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: First describe the image: the attached figure shows three congruent squares arranged in a triangular array: the two lower squares are side by side on the left and right, and share a vertical edge in the middle; one upper square is placed on the upper edges of the two lower squares, and is centered with this common vertical edge as the axis of symmetry. The three vertices of the dashed triangle correspond to the centers of the three squares. Then reason: let the side length of each square be s. Put the common vertical edge of the two lower squares at x=0, and put the upper edge at y=0, then the centers of the two lower squares are (-s/2,-s/2) and (s/2,-s/2), respectively, and the center of the upper square is (0,s/2). For the triangle formed by these three centers, its horizontal base length is s, and its vertical height is also s, so the area is (1/2)s^2. The problem gives this area as 100, therefore (1/2)s^2=100, obtaining s^2=200. The area of one square is exactly s^2.

method.method_draft: Use a coordinate setup. From the image, read that the two bottom congruent squares share a vertical side, and the top congruent square is centered over that shared side with its bottom edge resting on the top edges of the two lower squares. Let the side length of each square be s. Place the shared vertical edge of the bottom squares on x=0 and their top edge on y=0. Then the centers of the lower squares are (-s/2,-s/2) and (s/2,-s/2), while the center of the top square is (0,s/2). The triangle formed by these centers has horizontal base length s and vertical height s, so its area is (1/2)s^2. The text says this area is 100, so (1/2)s^2=100 and the area of one square is s^2=200.

From the image, observe that the segment joining the centers of the two bottom squares is horizontal and spans exactly one square side length s, because the centers of adjacent congruent squares are one side length apart. The perpendicular distance from the top square’s center to that horizontal segment is also s: it is s/2 down from the top square center to the common top edge of the lower squares, plus s/2 more down to the centers of the lower squares. Therefore the dashed center-triangle has base s and height s, so it occupies exactly half the area of a square of side s. Since the text gives the triangle area as 100, the square area must be twice that, 200.
